cards.question: Define: amplitude
cards.answer: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its rest position.
cards.explanation: Amplitude shows how far the wave moves from the middle/rest position.
cards.source: CGP KS3 Science syllabus map Year 9 Topic 6 Wave properties; Oak waves lessons

cards.question: Define: wavelength
cards.answer: Wavelength is the distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, such as crest to crest.
cards.explanation: Crest-to-crest or trough-to-trough are common ways to measure wavelength.
cards.source: CGP KS3 Science syllabus map Year 9 Topic 6 Wave properties; Oak waves lessons

cards.question: Define: frequency
cards.answer: Frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
cards.explanation: 1 Hz means one complete wave per second.
cards.source: CGP KS3 Science syllabus map Year 9 Topic 6 Wave properties; Oak waves lessons

cards.question: Which equation links wave speed, frequency and wavelength?
cards.answer: C

cards.question: A wave has frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 2 m. Calculate its speed.
cards.answer: 10 m/s
cards.explanation: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength = 5 × 2 = 10 m/s.

cards.question: A wave travels at 12 m/s and has wavelength 3 m. Calculate its frequency.
cards.answer: 4 Hz

cards.question: Describe a transverse wave.
cards.answer: In a transverse wave, the vibration is at right angles to the direction of energy transfer.
cards.explanation: Water waves are a common KS3 example of transverse waves.

cards.question: Describe a longitudinal wave.

cards.question: What happens to the particles as a sound wave travels through air?
cards.answer: The particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction the sound wave travels; the particles do not travel all the way with the sound.

cards.question: Explain why sound usually travels faster in solids than in gases.
cards.answer: Particles in solids are closer together and strongly linked, so vibrations are passed on more quickly.

cards.question: How could an echo method be used to estimate the speed of sound?
cards.answer: Make a sharp sound near a wall, time how long it takes to hear the echo, then use distance travelled divided by time. The sound travels to the wall and back.
cards.explanation: The distance is twice the distance from the sound source to the wall.

cards.question: Define: breathing
cards.answer: Breathing is the movement of air into and out of the lungs.
cards.explanation: Breathing is a physical movement of air, not the same as cellular respiration.

cards.question: Define: gas exchange
cards.answer: Gas exchange is the movement of oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out of the blood at the lungs.
cards.explanation: At the alveoli, oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse in opposite directions.

cards.question: Describe the difference between breathing and cellular respiration.

notes.title: Wave properties
notes.summary: Waves transfer energy. Key wave properties include amplitude, wavelength, frequency and wave speed.
keyPoints: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position.
Wavelength is the distance between matching points on neighbouring waves.
Frequency is the number of complete waves each second, measured in hertz.
Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.
Transverse waves vibrate at right angles to the energy transfer direction.
Longitudinal waves vibrate parallel to the energy transfer direction.
Sound is a longitudinal wave and needs a material medium.

commonMistakes.wrong: The particles travel all the way with the wave.
commonMistakes.correct: Particles vibrate around positions while energy is transferred.
commonMistakes.why: This is especially important for water and sound waves.
Air particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the wave direction.
Wave speed depends on the medium, not loudness.

example.question: A wave has f = 4 Hz and λ = 3 m. Calculate speed.

notes.explanation: For wave calculations, identify the two known quantities, write the wave-speed equation, then substitute values with units. For explanations, say what vibrates and which way energy is transferred.
notes.memoryHook: v = fλ: speed is frequency times wavelength.
notes.selfCheck: Can you define amplitude, wavelength and frequency without looking?
notes.sentenceStarter: This is a ___ wave because the vibration is ___.
notes.practicePrompt: Do one vocabulary card, one wave-speed calculation and one transverse/longitudinal comparison.

notes.title: Breathing and gas exchange
notes.summary: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Gas exchange moves oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out of the blood at the alveoli.
keyPoints: Breathing is ventilation: moving air into and out of the lungs.
Respiration is a chemical process in cells that releases energy from glucose.
Oxygen diffuses from alveoli into the blood.
Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.
Alveoli have thin walls and a large surface area for fast diffusion.
Breathing rate increases during exercise to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide faster.

commonMistakes.wrong: Breathing and respiration mean the same thing.
commonMistakes.correct: Breathing moves air; respiration releases energy in cells.
commonMistakes.why: They are linked but not identical.

commonMistakes.wrong: Carbon dioxide is breathed in for respiration.
commonMistakes.correct: Oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration; carbon dioxide is a waste product.
commonMistakes.why: Carbon dioxide is removed at the lungs.

commonMistakes.wrong: Alveoli have thick walls for protection.
commonMistakes.correct: Alveoli have thin walls for short diffusion distance.
commonMistakes.why: Thin walls speed up gas exchange.

example.question: What moves where at the alveoli?
example.answer: Oxygen moves into the blood; carbon dioxide moves into the alveoli.

notes.explanation: Strong gas-exchange answers use the words oxygen, carbon dioxide, alveoli, blood and diffusion. Strong breathing-mechanics answers use volume and pressure.
notes.memoryHook: Breathing moves air; respiration releases energy.
notes.selfCheck: Can you explain why exercise increases breathing rate?
notes.practicePrompt: Answer one card on breathing mechanics and one on alveoli adaptations.

notes.title: Anaerobic respiration
notes.summary: Anaerobic respiration releases energy without oxygen. In humans it produces lactic acid; in yeast it produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
keyPoints: Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water.
Anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen.
In human muscles: glucose -> lactic acid.
In yeast: glucose -> ethanol + carbon dioxide.
Fermentation is anaerobic respiration in microorganisms.
Anaerobic respiration releases less energy than aerobic respiration.
During vigorous exercise, muscles may use anaerobic respiration when oxygen supply is not enough.

commonMistakes.wrong: Anaerobic respiration in humans makes carbon dioxide and ethanol.
commonMistakes.correct: In humans it produces lactic acid.
commonMistakes.why: Yeast fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

commonMistakes.wrong: Anaerobic respiration releases more energy than aerobic respiration.
commonMistakes.correct: Aerobic respiration releases more energy from glucose.
commonMistakes.why: Oxygen allows more complete breakdown of glucose.

example.question: What is the yeast fermentation word summary?

notes.explanation: Be clear which organism is being discussed. Human anaerobic respiration and yeast fermentation have different products.
notes.memoryHook: Human hard exercise: lactic acid. Yeast fermentation: ethanol + CO₂.
notes.selfCheck: Can you compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in oxygen use, products and energy released?
notes.practicePrompt: Answer one human respiration card and one yeast fermentation card.
